opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I have enormous respect for them. I think there's this narrative that you have to be grinding eighty-hour weeks to have impact, and I just don't think that's true. Some of the most valuable people I worked with at Google were people who'd been there for ten or fifteen years, had kids, went home at five or six, and were incredibly effective in the hours they were there.

What they had was taste and context. They knew where the bodies were buried in the codebase, they knew which experiments were worth running and which ones were going to waste three weeks of compute, and they could look at a design and tell you in ten minutes why it wouldn't scale. That kind of judgment compounds over years, and it doesn't really come from hours logged. It comes from having seen a lot of things fail.

For me personally, at the stage I was at, working really long hours made sense. I was young, I didn't have those commitments, and I was trying to accumulate that context as fast as I could. Hours were basically my way of compressing the learning curve. But I'd never look at someone making a different trade-off and think less of them. If anything, the people who sustain a career over decades while having a full life are playing a longer game, and often a smarter one.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that it's one or the other. The best senior people I knew were really intentional with their time. They protected deep work, they said no to a lot of meetings, and they were generous mentors, which multiplies their impact through everyone around them. That's a very different kind of leverage from just being the person in the office at midnight, and organizations that only reward the midnight person are missing a lot.

r001.rationale: It credits experienced Google colleagues’ impact to their taste, context, and judgment about the codebase, experiments, and designs.

r002.rationale: It does not state that society depends on engineers maintaining large, complex systems.

r003.rationale: It does not compare public recognition of system maintenance with recognition of AI work.

r004.rationale: Douglas says that at his younger stage he had no such commitments, which made working long hours make sense for him.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's completely legitimate, and honestly I have a lot of respect for it. The framing where someone who goes home at six is somehow less serious or less committed, I just don't think that holds up when you actually look at who's doing great work.

Some of the most impactful people I've worked with at Google are people with kids who are extremely disciplined about their time. They're not in the building at eleven at night, but what they do between nine and five is incredibly focused. They've developed this ruthless prioritization, partly because they have to. They know exactly which problems matter and they don't waste cycles on things that don't. And the experience compounds. Someone who's been doing this for fifteen years has intuition about what's going to work that lets them skip a lot of the thrashing that younger people like me go through.

Now, I'll be honest about my own situation. I work a lot. I find it really fun, I'm at a stage of life where I don't have those obligations, and I think there's a genuine advantage to just putting more hours in when you're in a field that's moving this fast. Every week there's some new result and the people who are deeply immersed catch on faster. So I don't want to pretend hours don't matter at all. They do, especially early on when you're building the foundation.

But I think the mistake is treating it as the only variable. The question isn't how many hours someone works, it's what they produce and what they enable other people to produce. A senior engineer who spends an afternoon unblocking three people on their team, and then goes to pick up their kids, has probably done more for the project than someone grinding alone until midnight on the wrong thing.

And there's a longevity piece. This is a long game. The people who've been in the field for twenty years and are still sharp and still curious mostly didn't get there by burning themselves out at thirty. So I'd much rather have a team that's sustainable and sane than one that's optimizing for visible intensity. The intensity should go into the problem, not into performing commitment.

r001.rationale: The response credits experienced engineers’ intuition and prioritization to their years of experience, but does not connect their high leverage to expertise in the systems they work on.

r002.rationale: It does not state that society depends on engineers maintaining large, complex systems.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between public recognition for system maintenance and AI work.

r004.rationale: The speaker says he works a lot because he finds it fun and is at a stage of life without those obligations, conveying that long hours currently entail fewer personal sacrifices.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a completely reasonable choice. Someone can be an excellent engineer and care deeply about their work while also wanting to get home to their kids. Those aren’t contradictory things. And hours aren’t the same as contribution—an experienced engineer who knows which approach is going to fail can save everyone else weeks of work.

There are projects where speed matters enormously, and you want a team that’s excited to work intensely. But that’s a question of matching people to the work, not a reason to look down on someone for having different priorities.
